items.title: Pensions and retirement
items.intro: When you can take your pensions, and the ways to take an income from them.
body: Most people can take money from a personal or workplace pension from 55. That age is due to rise to 57 on 6 April 2028.
Your State Pension age depends on when you were born, and you can check yours on GOV.UK.
You can usually take a quarter of a pension tax-free, and the rest is taxed as income when you take it. The choices about how you take it are hard to undo, so they're worth understanding first.
Pension Wise, from the government's MoneyHelper service, offers a free appointment about your options if you're 50 or over.
help: Find out what all your pensions are worth today, and what they charge
Work out when you could stop work, and the income you'd have
Choose how to take an income, and review it each year

sources.label: GOV.UK: Increasing normal minimum pension age

items.title: Inheritance tax
items.intro: What your estate might owe, and what changes from April 2027.
body: Inheritance tax is usually charged at 40% on the part of an estate above £325,000. A further £175,000 can apply when a home passes to children or grandchildren.
Anything left to a husband, wife or civil partner is usually free of inheritance tax, and unused allowances can pass to them.
From 6 April 2027, most unused pension funds will count as part of an estate for inheritance tax.
help: Set out what your estate is made of, and what it might owe
Look at gifts, trusts and how your pensions are left
Work with your solicitor on your will

items.title: Protection
items.intro: What would happen to your family's money if you couldn't work, or died.
body: Life cover pays a sum if you die during the policy. Income protection pays part of your income if illness or injury stops you working. Critical illness cover pays a sum if you're diagnosed with a condition the policy lists.
Many employers include some cover, so it's worth knowing what you have before buying more.
help: Check the cover you already have through work and elsewhere
Write policies in trust where that suits you

items.title: Mortgages
items.intro: Buying, remortgaging, and borrowing later in life.
body: Your home may be repossessed if you do not keep up repayments on your mortgage.
When a fixed rate ends, most mortgages move to the lender's standard variable rate, so it's worth looking at the choices a few months before.
help: Search the market for a mortgage that suits you
Plan a remortgage before your fixed rate ends
Fit borrowing in with your pension and retirement plans

items.title: Business owners
items.intro: Paying yourself well, and planning for the day you sell.
body: A company can pay into its directors' pensions, and those payments are usually treated as a business expense.
When you sell a business, Business Asset Disposal Relief can lower the Capital Gains Tax on qualifying gains, up to a lifetime limit.
help: Plan pension contributions through your company
Work with your accountant before a sale
Plan what to do with the money afterwards

items.title: Later life and care
items.intro: Paying for care, and helping a parent with their money.
body: Whether the council helps with care costs depends on the person's needs, income and savings. The rules differ in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
A lasting power of attorney lets someone you trust make decisions for you if you can't. It has to be made while you still can.
help: Set out the ways to pay for care, and what each costs
Help a family member make a lasting power of attorney with their solicitor
Look after the money once care begins

guides.title: Guides
guides.intro: What to do, in order, at the moments that change your money.

items.title: Retiring in the next five years
items.intro: The steps to take, from five years out to your last day.

steps.title: Find every pension
steps.text: List each employer and personal pension, and ask each for its current value and charges.

steps.title: Get your State Pension forecast
steps.text: Check how much you're due and when on GOV.UK, and whether gaps can be filled.

steps.title: Work out what you'll spend
steps.text: A simple monthly budget for the first years of retirement is enough to start.

steps.title: Decide how to take an income
steps.text: Take guidance or advice before you take money out; some choices can't be undone.

items.title: Inheriting money
items.intro: What to do in the first months after an inheritance.

steps.title: Wait for the estate to settle
steps.text: The executors pay any tax and debts first, which can take many months.

steps.title: Keep it safe meanwhile
steps.text: An easy-access account covered by the FSCS is a good place while you decide.

steps.title: Think about your own will
steps.text: An inheritance can change what you'd want to leave, and to whom.

items.title: When a parent needs care
items.intro: The order to do things in when care is coming.

steps.title: Ask for a needs assessment
steps.text: The council assesses care needs for free, whoever ends up paying.

steps.title: Check for a lasting power of attorney
steps.text: If there isn't one and your parent can still make one, make it now.

steps.title: Work out how care is paid for
steps.text: Income, savings and sometimes the home all count; get advice before selling anything.

journal.title: Journal

items.title: Pensions and inheritance tax from April 2027
items.summary: Most unused pensions will count towards an estate. What that means for how you leave yours.
body: From 6 April 2027, most unused pension funds will count towards an estate for inheritance tax.
If you were planning to leave your pension untouched to pass it on, it's worth looking again at the order you draw on your savings, and at who your pensions go to.
items.author: Daniel Okafor

items.title: The pension age is rising to 57
items.summary: From 6 April 2028, most people will have to wait until 57 to take money from a pension.
body: The earliest age most people can take money from a personal or workplace pension rises from 55 to 57 on 6 April 2028.
Some schemes give members a protected lower age. Ask your scheme whether yours does before you plan around it.

blocks.heading: Why we're independent

Every client has one adviser who knows their affairs, and a planner who works alongside them.
